In [[algebra]], '''Weyl's theorem on complete reducibility''' is a fundamental result in the theory of [[Lie algebra representation]]s (specifically in the [[representation theory of semisimple Lie algebras]]). Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> be a [[semisimple Lie algebra]] over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] of [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] zero. The theorem states that every finite-dimensional module over <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is [[semisimple representation|semisimple]] as a module (i.e., a direct sum of simple modules.)<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorem 10.9</ref>

== The enveloping algebra is semisimple ==
Weyl's theorem implies (in fact is equivalent to) that the [[enveloping algebra of a representation|enveloping algebra of a finite-dimensional representation]] is a [[semisimple ring]] in the following way.

Given a finite-dimensional Lie algebra representation <math>\pi: \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(V)</math>, let <math>A \subset \operatorname{End}(V)</math> be the associative subalgebra of the endomorphism algebra of ''V'' generated by <math>\pi(\mathfrak g)</math>. The ring ''A'' is called the enveloping algebra of <math>\pi</math>. If <math>\pi</math> is semisimple, then ''A'' is semisimple.<ref>{{harvnb|Jacobson|1979|loc=Ch. II, § 5, Theorem 10.}}</ref> (Proof: Since ''A'' is a finite-dimensional algebra, it is an [[Artinian ring]]; in particular, the [[Jacobson radical]] ''J'' is nilpotent. If ''V'' is simple, then <math>JV \subset V</math> implies that <math>JV = 0</math>. In general, ''J'' kills each simple submodule of ''V''; in particular, ''J'' kills ''V'' and so ''J'' is zero.) Conversely, if ''A'' is semisimple, then ''V'' is a semisimple ''A''-module; i.e., semisimple as a <math>\mathfrak g</math>-module. (Note that a module over a semisimple ring is semisimple since a module is a quotient of a [[free module]] and "semisimple" is preserved under the free and quotient constructions.)

== Application: preservation of Jordan decomposition ==
Here is a typical application.<ref>{{harvnb|Jacobson|1979|loc=Ch. III, § 11, Theorem 17.}}</ref>

{{math_theorem|name=Proposition|math_statement=Let <math>\mathfrak g</math> be a semisimple finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero and <math>x</math> an element of <math>\mathfrak g</math>.{{efn|Editorial note: this fact is usually stated for a field of characteristic zero, but the proof needs only that the base field be perfect.}}
# There exists a unique pair of elements <math>x_s, x_n</math> in <math>\mathfrak g</math> such that <math>x = x_s + x_n</math>, <math>\operatorname{ad}(x_s)</math> is semisimple, <math>\operatorname{ad}(x_n)</math> is nilpotent and <math>[x_s, x_n] = 0</math>.
# If <math>\pi : \mathfrak{g} \to \mathfrak{gl}(V)</math> is a finite-dimensional representation, then <math>\pi(x)_s = \pi(x_s)</math> and <math>\pi(x)_n = \pi(x_n)</math>, where <math>\pi(x)_s, \pi(x)_n</math> denote the Jordan decomposition of the semisimple and nilpotent parts of the endomorphism <math>\pi(x)</math>.
In short, the semisimple and nilpotent parts of an element of <math>\mathfrak g</math> are well-defined and are determined independent of a faithful finite-dimensional representation.}}

''Proof'': First we prove the special case of (i) and (ii) when <math>\pi</math> is the inclusion; i.e., <math>\mathfrak g</math> is a subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak{gl}_n = \mathfrak{gl}(V)</math>. Let <math>x = S + N</math> be the Jordan decomposition of the endomorphism <math>x</math>, where <math>S, N</math> are semisimple and nilpotent endomorphisms in <math>\mathfrak{gl}_n</math>. Now, <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{gl}_n}(x)</math> also has the Jordan decomposition, which can be shown (see [[Jordan–Chevalley decomposition#Preservation under representations|Jordan–Chevalley decomposition]]) to respect the above Jordan decomposition; i.e., <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{gl}_n}(S), \operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{gl}_n}(N)</math> are the semisimple and nilpotent parts of <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{gl}_n}(x)</math>. Since <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{gl}_n}(S), \operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{gl}_n}(N)</math> are polynomials in <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{gl}_n}(x)</math> then, we see <math>\operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{gl}_n}(S), \operatorname{ad}_{\mathfrak{gl}_n}(N) : \mathfrak g \to \mathfrak g</math>. Thus, they are derivations of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>. Since <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is semisimple, we can find elements <math>s, n</math> in <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> such that <math>[y, S] = [y, s], y \in \mathfrak{g}</math> and similarly for <math>n</math>. Now, let ''A'' be the enveloping algebra of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>; i.e., the subalgebra of the endomorphism algebra of ''V'' generated by <math>\mathfrak g</math>. As noted above, ''A'' has zero Jacobson radical. Since <math>[y, N - n] = 0</math>, we see that <math>N - n</math> is a nilpotent element in the center of ''A''. But, in general, a central nilpotent belongs to the Jacobson radical; hence, <math>N = n</math> and thus also <math>S = s</math>. This proves the special case.

In general, <math>\pi(x)</math> is semisimple (resp. nilpotent) when <math>\operatorname{ad}(x)</math> is semisimple (resp. nilpotent).{{clarify|why?|date=October 2020}} This immediately gives (i) and (ii). <math>\square</math>

== Proofs ==
=== Analytic proof ===
Weyl's original proof (for complex semisimple Lie algebras) was analytic in nature: it famously used the [[unitarian trick]]. Specifically, one can show that every complex semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is the complexification of the Lie algebra of a simply connected compact [[Lie group]] <math>K</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Knapp|2002}} Theorem 6.11</ref> (If, for example, <math>\mathfrak{g}=\mathrm{sl}(n;\mathbb{C})</math>, then <math>K=\mathrm{SU}(n)</math>.) Given a representation <math>\pi</math> of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> on a [[vector space]] <math>V,</math> one can first restrict <math>\pi</math> to the Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{k}</math> of <math>K</math>. Then, [[Lie_group–Lie_algebra_correspondence#The_correspondence|since <math>K</math> is simply connected]],<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorem 5.10</ref> there is an associated representation <math>\Pi</math> of <math>K</math>. Integration over <math>K</math> produces an inner product on <math>V</math> for which <math>\Pi</math> is unitary.<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorem 4.28</ref> Complete reducibility of <math>\Pi</math> is then immediate and elementary arguments show that the original representation <math>\pi</math> of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is also completely reducible.

===Algebraic proof 1===
Let <math>(\pi, V)</math> be a finite-dimensional representation of a Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math> over a field of characteristic zero. The theorem is an easy consequence of [[Whitehead's lemma (Lie algebra)|Whitehead's lemma]], which says <math>V \to \operatorname{Der}(\mathfrak g, V), v \mapsto \cdot v</math> is surjective, where a linear map <math>f: \mathfrak g \to V</math> is a [[derivation (algebra)|derivation]] if <math>f([x, y]) = x \cdot f(y) - y \cdot f(x)</math>. The proof is essentially due to Whitehead.<ref>{{harvnb|Jacobson|1979|loc=Ch. III, § 7.}}</ref>

Let <math>W \subset V</math> be a subrepresentation. Consider the vector subspace <math>L_W \subset \operatorname{End}(V)</math> that consists of all linear maps <math>t: V \to V</math> such that <math>t(V) \subset W</math> and <math>t(W) = 0</math>. It has a structure of a <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-module given by: for <math>x \in \mathfrak{g}, t \in L_W</math>,
:<math>x \cdot t = [\pi(x), t]</math>.
Now, pick some projection <math>p : V \to V</math> onto ''W'' and consider <math>f : \mathfrak{g} \to L_W</math> given by <math>f(x) = [p, \pi(x)]</math>. Since <math>f</math> is a derivation, by Whitehead's lemma, we can write <math>f(x) = x \cdot t</math> for some <math>t \in L_W</math>. We then have <math>[\pi(x), p + t] = 0, x \in \mathfrak{g}</math>; that is to say <math>p + t</math> is <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>-linear. Also, as ''t'' kills <math>W</math>, <math>p + t</math> is an idempotent such that <math>(p + t)(V) = W</math>. The kernel of <math>p + t</math> is then a complementary representation to <math>W</math>. <math>\square</math>

=== Algebraic proof 2 ===
[[Whitehead's lemma (Lie algebra)|Whitehead's lemma]] is typically proved by means of the [[Casimir_element#Quadratic_Casimir_element|quadratic Casimir element]] of the [[universal enveloping algebra]],<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Section 10.3</ref> and there is also a proof of the theorem that uses the Casimir element directly instead of Whitehead's lemma.<!-- The proof is due to whom? -->

Since the quadratic Casimir element <math>C</math> is in the center of the universal enveloping algebra, [[Schur's lemma]] tells us that <math>C</math> acts as multiple <math>c_\lambda</math> of the identity in the irreducible representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> with highest weight <math>\lambda</math>. A key point is to establish that <math>c_\lambda</math> is ''nonzero'' whenever the representation is nontrivial. This can be done by a general argument <ref>{{harvnb|Humphreys|1973}} Section 6.2</ref> or by the [[Casimir_element#Eigenvalues|explicit formula]] for <math>c_\lambda</math>.

Consider a very special case of the theorem on complete reducibility: the case where a representation <math>V</math> contains a nontrivial, irreducible, invariant subspace <math>W</math> of codimension one. Let <math>C_V</math> denote the action of <math>C</math> on <math>V</math>. Since <math>V</math> is not irreducible, <math>C_V</math> is not necessarily a multiple of the identity, but it is a self-intertwining operator for <math>V</math>. Then the restriction of <math>C_V</math> to <math>W</math> is a nonzero multiple of the identity. But since the quotient <math>V/W</math> is a one dimensional—and therefore trivial—representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, the action of <math>C</math> on the quotient is trivial. It then easily follows that <math>C_V</math> must have a nonzero kernel—and the kernel is an invariant subspace, since <math>C_V</math> is a self-intertwiner. The kernel is then a one-dimensional invariant subspace, whose intersection with <math>W</math> is zero. Thus, <math>\mathrm{ker}(C_V)</math> is an invariant complement to <math>W</math>, so that <math>V</math> decomposes as a direct sum of irreducible subspaces:
:<math>V=W\oplus\mathrm{ker}(C_V)</math>.

Although this establishes only a very special case of the desired result, this step is actually the critical one in the general argument.

=== Algebraic proof 3 ===
The theorem can be deduced from the theory of [[Verma module]]s, which characterizes a simple module as a quotient of a Verma module by a [[maximal submodule]].<ref>{{harvnb|Kac|1990|loc=Lemma 9.5.}}</ref> This approach has an advantage that it can be used to weaken the finite-dimensionality assumptions (on algebra and representation).

Let <math>V</math> be a finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak g</math> over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let <math>\mathfrak b = \mathfrak{h} \oplus \mathfrak{n}_+ \subset \mathfrak{g}</math> be the [[Borel subalgebra]] determined by a choice of a Cartan subalgebra and positive roots. Let <math>V^0 = \{ v \in V | \mathfrak{n}_+(v) = 0 \}</math>. Then <math>V^0</math> is an <math>\mathfrak h</math>-module and thus has the <math>\mathfrak h</math>-weight space decomposition:
:<math>V^0 = \bigoplus_{\lambda \in L} V^0_{\lambda}</math>
where <math>L \subset \mathfrak{h}^*</math>. For each <math>\lambda \in L</math>, pick <math>0 \ne v_{\lambda} \in V_{\lambda}</math> and <math>V^{\lambda} \subset V</math> the <math>\mathfrak g</math>-submodule generated by <math>v_{\lambda}</math> and <math>V' \subset V</math> the <math>\mathfrak g</math>-submodule generated by <math>V^0</math>. We claim: <math>V = V'</math>. Suppose <math>V \ne V'</math>. By [[Lie's theorem]], there exists a <math>\mathfrak{b}</math>-weight vector in <math>V/V'</math>; thus, we can find an <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>-weight vector <math>v</math> such that <math>0 \ne e_i(v) \in V'</math> for some <math>e_i</math> among the [[Chevalley generators]]. Now, <math>e_i(v)</math> has weight <math>\mu + \alpha_i</math>. Since <math>L</math> is partially ordered, there is a <math>\lambda \in L</math> such that <math>\lambda \ge \mu + \alpha_i</math>; i.e., <math>\lambda > \mu</math>. But this is a contradiction since <math>\lambda, \mu</math> are both primitive weights (it is known that the primitive weights are incomparable.{{clarify|More details should be given on this matter|date=September 2020}}). Similarly, each <math>V^{\lambda}</math> is simple as a <math>\mathfrak g</math>-module. Indeed, if it is not simple, then, for some <math>\mu < \lambda</math>, <math>V^0_{\mu}</math> contains some nonzero vector that is not a highest-weight vector; again a contradiction.{{clarify|More explanation|date=September 2020}} <math>\square</math>
